# Brief: fix the interview scoring before the autumn recruitment round

Two panels interviewing for the same role are producing scores a point and a
half apart on the same candidates, and we only know that because one candidate
was accidentally seen twice. The autumn round is forty interviews across six
panels. I want the scoring calibration sorted before it starts rather than
discovered afterwards in the offer statistics.

## What we know

We reran the accident deliberately: three candidates who consented were seen by
both panels in the same week. The gap held. One panel is systematically
generous on the communication criterion and systematically harsh on the
technical one; the other is the reverse. The average is similar, which is why
nobody noticed for two rounds, and the average is exactly what does not matter
to an individual candidate.

Reading the score sheets afterwards, the disagreement is not really about the
candidates. It is about what a 4 means. One panel treats 4 as "clearly meets the
bar" and reserves 5 for exceptional. The other treats 5 as "meets the bar" and
never uses anything below 3, so their range is compressed into two points.

## What I want

- A shared definition of each point on the scale, written as observable
  behaviour rather than as adjectives. "Explained a trade-off without being
  asked" is checkable. "Good communicator" is not, and it is where the drift
  gets in.
- A calibration session before the round, with everybody scoring the same two
  recorded interviews and the results compared in the room. I would rather the
  argument happen there than in a hiring decision.
- A light check during the round — the score distributions by panel, looked at
  weekly, so a panel drifting apart from the others is visible while there are
  still interviews left to correct.
- A view on whether we need six panels at all. Fewer panels seeing more
  candidates is the simplest way to make scores comparable, and it costs
  calendar time we may or may not have.

## Constraints

Nobody is being trained for a day. Two hours in total, and it has to be
useful to the four people who have done this for years as well as to the two who
have not done it at all. The scale itself cannot change — it is on the applicant
tracking system and shared with two other departments.

## What I do not want

A weighting model. The last time a scoring problem came to a working group it
returned a spreadsheet with per-criterion weights, and the discussion became
about the weights. The problem is that we do not agree what the numbers mean,
and no amount of arithmetic downstream fixes that.

## Deliverable

The scale definitions on one page, a two-hour session designed and booked, and a
weekly distribution check somebody owns by name. Ready two weeks before the
first interview, so there is room to fix what the session turns up.
